title: Stains, oils, sealers and recoating: finish control and handover
audience: Timber floor restoration workers who apply stains, oils or sealers, and who walk the floor with the client at handover.
learningOutcomes: Confirm that a finish is compatible with the sanded timber and the scope before applying it.
Apply thin coats and observe the drying, recoat and cure times stated on the product label.
Walk the floor against the acceptance criteria and hand over care instructions with a signed record.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: WorkSafe Victoria, Wood dust: health hazards and control (reviewed 17 April 2026).

instruction.heading: Confirm compatibility and the approved finish
instruction.body: The finish must be the one stated in the approved scope and must be compatible with the sanded timber and any finish that remains. Confirm the product name, the batch and the SDS. Test the stain or finish on an offcut or an inconspicuous area first, and record the result, because the same product can look different on different timbers and under different light. Where the client has chosen the colour, record the choice and the test result they accepted.

instruction.heading: Applying thin coats
instruction.body: Apply thin coats as the product label states. Thick coats do not dry faster, and they can trap solvent, soften, or show brush or roller marks. Sand between coats only where the label allows it, and remove dust with the damp method from “Dust control: extraction, wet cleaning and safe clean-up” before the next coat, as the wood dust guidance recommends. Keep the room ventilated and free of ignition sources during application, as set out in “Solvents, stains, finishes and fire risk in timber restoration”. Do not pool finish in corners or at joints.

instruction.heading: Drying, recoat and cure
instruction.body: Use the drying and recoat times stated on the label, adjusted for the actual conditions only where the manufacturer allows. Record the time each coat was applied and when the next coat was started. Restrict foot traffic until the cure time stated by the manufacturer has passed. A floor that feels dry can still be soft underneath. Furniture is returned only after the stated cure time.

instruction.heading: Slip and traffic risk
instruction.body: Freshly coated floors can be slippery, and footprints and furniture can mark them. Post warning signs, control access and keep the area clear until the stated drying time has passed.

instruction.heading: Walkthrough and handover
instruction.body: At handover, walk the floor with the client under raking light and check it against the acceptance criteria in the scope. Record any remaining defects, and agree in writing how they will be resolved. Hand over the manufacturer's care instructions for the finish, and the record of the products used. Ask the client to sign the handover record. The record is evidence of what was agreed, not a guarantee of how the floor will look in future.

procedure: Confirm the finish against the scope and its compatibility with the sanded timber, and record the product, batch and SDS.
Test the finish on an offcut or inconspicuous area, and record the result and any client acceptance.
Apply thin coats as the label states, with ventilation and ignition controls in place.
Record the time of each coat and the drying and recoat times, and restrict access until cure.
Post warnings and keep the floor clear of foot traffic and furniture until the cure time has passed.
Walk the floor with the client under raking light against the acceptance criteria, and record remaining defects.
Hand over the care instructions and obtain the client's signature on the handover record.

workedExamples.situation: A client wants a dark stain applied over a floor that was previously finished with an oil. The stain test on an offcut looks uneven, and the client wants the whole floor done today.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not apply the stain to the whole floor on the offcut result. The uneven test and the previous oil finish raise a compatibility question that must be checked against the product information. Record the test result and the client's acceptance in writing, or agree a different approach. Do not promise an even colour on old timber. Apply the stain only after the client has accepted the test and the product has been confirmed compatible.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved finish products with labels and SDS
Applicators such as brushes, rollers or pads, as the product label states
Offcut for the colour and compatibility test

commonErrors.error: Applying thick coats to speed up drying.
commonErrors.prevention: Apply thin coats as the label states, and keep to the stated times.

commonErrors.error: Allowing foot traffic or furniture before the cure time has passed.
commonErrors.prevention: Restrict access and post signs until the stated cure time.

commonErrors.error: Applying a film finish over an oil finish without checking compatibility.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm compatibility with the product information and test first.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Solvent and finish vapours: the SDS controls and the ventilation in “Solvents, stains, finishes and fire risk in timber restoration” apply to all application work.

qualityStandard: The finish matches the scope and its compatibility is recorded.
A test result is recorded and accepted by the client before the whole floor is finished.
The floor is walked with the client against the acceptance criteria before handover, and the handover is signed.
documentationEvidence: Finish record with product, batch, number of coats and times
Test record on offcut, with client acceptance
Handover record signed by the client
summary: Confirm compatibility and test the finish before the whole floor.
Apply thin coats, keep to the label times, and restrict access until cure.
Walk the floor with the client against the acceptance criteria, and record what is agreed.
referencesAtEnd: Official sources to recheck before any job: WorkSafe Victoria, Wood dust: health hazards and control (reviewed 17 April 2026); AS 4586.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why test a finish on an offcut or inconspicuous area?
options: To save money on the materials
To remove the need for the product label
To avoid the client and the owner
To check compatibility and the result

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the safer approach to coating a floor?
options: Thin coats applied as the label states
Thick coats for speed on the floor
Skipping the label on the tin altogether
Walking on the floor at once after coat

knowledgeChecks.question: How should a freshly finished floor be handled?
options: Walked on immediately by the crew and the client
Access restricted until the stated cure time has passed
Left open to foot traffic at the door and the hall
Covered with wet carpet straight away on the floor

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the purpose of a walkthrough at handover?
options: To invoice faster for the job, the client, the team and the office today
To avoid writing records of the visit, the floor, the job and the client
To check the floor against the acceptance criteria and record any remaining defects
To remove the client's furniture from the room before the visit and the walk

knowledgeChecks.question: Which record shows what was agreed at handover?
options: A verbal understanding only, given on the day
The invoice alone, sent later on by email
A supplier's brochure for the floor finish
The signed handover record of what was agreed
